extraction.name: ChartQA
extraction.description: A large-scale benchmark for question answering about charts with visual and logical reasoning. It covers 9,608 human-written questions and 23,111 questions generated from human-written chart summaries. The benchmark consists of 20,882 charts curated from four different online sources (Statista, Pew Research, Our World In Data, OECD) to ensure variety in visual styles and topics. Questions focus on compositional and visual reasoning, including arithmetic and logical operations over chart data.
extraction.creator: Ahmed Masry, Do Xuan Long, Jia Qing Tan, Shafiq Joty, Enamul Hoque
extraction.publisher: York University, Canada; Nanyang Technological University, Singapore; Salesforce Research
extraction.citeAs: Masry, A., Long, D. X., Tan, J. Q., Joty, S., & Hoque, E. (2022). ChartQA: A Benchmark for Question Answering about Charts with Visual and Logical Reasoning. arXiv:2203.10244v1 [cs.CL].
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Charts were crawled from four different online sources: Statista (statista.com), Pew Research (pewresearch.org), Our World In Data or OWID (ourworldindata.org), and OECD (oecd.org). For the Pew dataset, only chart images were crawled since the underlying data tables are not available. For the other three sources, the underlying data tables, metadata (e.g., title, chart type), SVG files, and associated text descriptions were extracted. Bounding box information of different chart elements was extracted from SVG files to train data extraction models. Human-authored QA pairs were collected using Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT), and additional QA pairs were generated automatically from human-written chart summaries using a fine-tuned T5 model.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: For the Pew dataset, the underlying data tables are not available, so only chart images were crawled. Some machine-generated questions were found to be either incomplete or not answerable from the chart (e.g., questions requiring knowledge outside of the chart). A heuristic was applied to filter out such invalid questions, and the test set was manually cleaned by removing invalid questions.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Charts and associated data were collected from four online sources: Statista (economy, politics, industry topics), Pew Research (social and economic issues, demographic trends, public opinion), Our World In Data (global issues such as economy, finance, society), and OECD (reports and data analysis for policymaking). Human-written chart summaries from Statista were used to generate machine-based QA pairs.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: A T5 model was fine-tuned on the SQuAD QA dataset and applied to human-written chart summaries from Statista to automatically generate questions. The process involved two T5 models: one for answer extraction (trained on SQuAD passage-answer pairs) and one for answer-aware question generation (trained on SQuAD passage-answer-question triples). A heuristic filter was applied to remove questions where the answer could not be found in the chart data table. The test set of the machine-generated dataset was manually cleaned by removing invalid questions.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Charts were crawled from four sources. For Statista, Pew, OWID, and OECD, underlying data tables, metadata, SVG files, and associated text descriptions were extracted. Bounding box information of chart elements was extracted from SVG files. For machine-generated QA pairs, a heuristic filter was applied to remove questions where the answer could not be found in the chart data table. The dataset was randomly split into train, validation, and test sets for both ChartQA-H and ChartQA-M subsets.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human-authored QA pairs were collected via Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT). Workers were asked to provide two types of questions for each chart image: compositional questions (containing at least two mathematical/logical operations) and visual questions (referring to visual attributes such as color, height, and length of graphical marks). For each chart, workers provided two questions with answers. The same questions were then answered by another annotator. If both workers' answers exactly matched, the answer was considered correct. Otherwise, answers were manually checked to select the final correct answer. Workers were required to have an acceptance rate of 95% and at least 5,000 accomplished HITs, and were further filtered through a pre-test.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Agreement between crowd workers based on exact matches was 61.04%. A manual check of 500 random samples found agreement to be 78.55% when considering typos and lexical variations (e.g., '3$' vs '3 dollars', '86.33' vs '86.3'). For machine-generated QA pairs, 1,250 QA pairs were manually analyzed and 86.64% were found to be complete, answerable, and correct given the chart.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 2 questions per chart (human-authored); each question answered by at least 2 annotators
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Amazon Mechanical Turk workers with an acceptance rate of 95% and at least 5,000 accomplished HITs. Workers were compensated based on the minimum wage in the United States at the time ($7.25 USD per hour), receiving $0.60 USD per task (estimated 3-5 minutes per task). All annotations were anonymized to protect annotator privacy.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: T5 model fine-tuned on SQuAD for answer extraction and question generation; ChartOCR (Luo et al., 2021) extended for automatic chart data extraction; CRAFT model (Baek et al., 2019) for text recognition in chart elements; Mask R-CNN with Resnet-101 for visual feature extraction
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: Code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/vis-nlp/ChartQA. No explicit versioning, update schedule, or deprecation policy is described in the paper.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: No personal or sensitive human attributes are collected as part of this dataset. Annotator annotations were anonymized to protect privacy.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark is intended to advance Chart Question Answering systems that help users analyze data visualizations. The authors note that models can be abused to mislead the public about chart content and implications. The dataset covers topics including politics, economy, health, and society, with charts sourced from reputable organizations. The authors respected intellectual property rights by only using publicly available charts that comply with the terms and conditions of each source.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Politics is a common topic among all sources, particularly in the Pew dataset where nearly half of charts are about U.S. Politics & Policy (45.4%). Bar charts are the most common chart type across all datasets. Among bar charts, 79.4% were simple and 20.6% were complex. The dataset is constructed from four different sources, providing diverse topic coverage, but the distribution is not uniform across topics or chart types.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Most existing models cannot effectively handle nested arithmetic operations. Performance decreases when the gold data table is not provided, highlighting challenges in automatic data extraction from real-world charts with diverse styles. Current approaches for automatic data extraction are modular and combine deep learning and rule-based methods which are error-prone. Evaluation metrics for chart data extraction do not take extracted textual tokens into consideration. The benchmark focuses only on bar, line, and pie charts. Machine-generated questions may still contain invalid or unanswerable questions despite filtering (86.64% valid after filtering).
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, Validation, and Testing of Chart Question Answering (ChartQA) models. The benchmark is intended to serve as a starting point for research on visual and logical reasoning over charts. It can be used to evaluate models on compositional questions (requiring mathematical/logical operations) and visual questions (referring to visual attributes of chart elements). The dataset is split into training, validation, and test sets for both human-authored (ChartQA-H) and machine-generated (ChartQA-M) subsets.
